'''Huguette Delavault''' (15 January 1924 – 2 April 2003) was a French mathematician, specialising in [[mathematical physics]].<ref name="more">{{cite web|url=http://www.femmesetassociations.org/biodelavault.html |title=Huguette Delavault (née en 1924) |accessdate=2014-06-19 |url-status=bot: unknown |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20070927201436/http://www.femmesetassociations.org/biodelavault.html |archivedate=September 27, 2007 }} (in French), Caroline More, femmesetassociations.org, archived from the original on September 27, 2007.</ref><ref name="bua">[http://bu.univ-angers.fr/zone/Patrimoine/centre-des-archives-du-feminisme/archives-delavault-huguette-13-af Archives Huguette Delavault (13 AF)] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140714144454/http://bu.univ-angers.fr/zone/Patrimoine/centre-des-archives-du-feminisme/archives-delavault-huguette-13-af |date=2014-07-14 }} (in French), Univ. of Angers Library, retrieved 2014-06-18.</ref><ref name="gc">{{cite journal|title=Huguette Delavault 1924–2003|journal=Femmes & math|volume=7|year=2004|pages=71–79|url=https://www.numdam.org/item/RFM_2004__7__71_0/|last=Gondard-Cozette|first=Danièle|language=fr}}</ref> She co-founded [[Femmes et Sciences]].

==Early life and education==
Hugette Delavault was born on 15 January 1924, in [[Andilly, Charente-Maritime|Andilly, Charente-Maritime.]]<ref name="bua"/><ref name="gc"/> Her parents were both teachers.<ref name="more"/> She studied at a school for teachers, the École normale d'instituteurs in [[La Rochelle, France]], from 1940 to 1943, and then became a student at the École normale supérieure de Fontenay-aux-Roses from 1946 to 1949.<ref name="more"/><ref name="bua"/><ref name="gc"/> After interrupting her studies for health reasons,<ref name="gc"/> in 1952 she passed her [[agrégation]] in mathematics.<ref name="more"/><ref name="bua"/><ref name="gc"/> 

== Career ==
Delavault became a researcher at the [[French National Centre for Scientific Research]] (CNRS) from 1952 to 1958, while earning a doctorate in mathematics in 1957 from the [[University of Paris]] under the supervision of [[Henri Villat]]; her dissertation applied the [[Laplace transform]] and [[Hankel transform]] to the [[heat equation]] and [[Maxwell's equations]], using [[cylindrical coordinates]].<ref name="more" /><ref name="gc" /><ref>{{mathgenealogy|id=63649}}</ref> 

She became a researcher at the [[University of Rennes]] in 1958, was promoted to professor in 1962.<ref name="more" /> The university's mathematics department was unusual in 1960 because it had a relatively high percentage of women. There were fifteen professors and three of them were women. Delavault was one of them and the other two were [[Marie Charpentier]] and [[Paulette Libermann]]. Charpentier taught mechanics and Libermann was known for differential geometry.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Trois mathématiciennes à Rennes en 1960 |url=https://www.echosciences-paysdelaloire.fr/articles/trois-mathematiciennes-a-rennes-en-1960 |access-date=2026-06-10 |website=www.echosciences-paysdelaloire.fr}}</ref>

In 1970, Delavault became a professor at the [[École nationale supérieure d'ingénieurs de Caen]].<ref name="more" /><ref name="gc" /> She retired in 1984.<ref name="more" />

Delavault died on 2 April 2003.<ref name="gc"/>

==Activism and service==
From 1976 onward Delavault was a prominent activist for feminist causes, including popularising science and mathematics among women and providing equal opportunities for them both in the academy and in the public sector.<ref name="more"/><ref name="bua"/> 

She served as deputy director of the École normale supérieure de Fontenay-aux-Roses from 1976 to 1980, and was twice president of l'Association française des femmes diplômées des universités (the French association for university women).<ref name="more" /> 

Delavault co-founded [[Femmes et Sciences]] with [[Françoise Cyrot-Lackmann]], [[Claudine Hermann]], [[Françoise Gaspard]] and [[Colette Kreder]] in 2000.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Who are we? |url=https://www.femmesetsciences.fr/who-are-we |access-date=2026-02-16 |website=Femmes & Sciences |language=fr}}</ref>

==Awards and honours==
Delavault became an officer in the [[Ordre des Palmes Académiques|Order of Academic Palms]] in 1967. In 1971 she became a chevalier (knight) in the [[National Order of Merit (France)|French National Order of Merit]], and in 1995 a chevalier in the [[Legion of Honour]].<ref name="more"/><ref name="bua"/><ref name="gc"/>

There is a walkway on the University of Toulouse's campus which is named in her honour her.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Hommage à Huguette Delavault – Femmes et Mathématiques |url=https://femmes-et-maths.fr/hommage-a-huguette-delavault/ |access-date=2026-02-16 |language=fr-FR}}</ref>
